summary:
We developed CropSuite, an authentic multi-sensor crop feasibility and rotation decision engine engineered for smallholder farming in Rwanda’s complex highland topography.

Addressing the challenge of climate uncertainty, soil acidity, and land degradation, CropSuite replaces generic advice with a deterministic, transparent evaluation pipeline. It fuses NASA SRTM 30m elevation data to compute topographical slopes and enforce Rwandan conservation laws (amaterasi y'indinganire bench terracing), NASA SMAP topsoil (0–5 cm) moisture to protect seeds against lethal false-start rainy season desiccation, NASA POWER 8-year agro-climate distributions, FAO GAEZ v5 suitability grids, and localized MINAGRI/RAB soil profiles.

This project is critical because vulnerable smallholders cannot afford crop loss or irreversible topsoil erosion. By flagging hard biophysical barriers—such as landslides on unterraced slopes (>40%) or dry-season planting—and designing restorative crop rotations across Rwanda's seven staple crops, CropSuite transforms NASA Earth observation data into actionable, life-saving decisions on the ground.
details:
Project Details: CropSuite

What does CropSuite do and how does it work?

CropSuite is a web-based decision tool that helps farmers and extension workers in Rwanda check whether a crop will actually succeed on their land before planting, and what to rotate next season.

  1. User Input: A user selects their location (or picks a district preset), indicates whether their field has irrigation or bench terraces, chooses their candidate crops, previous crops, and sets their planting window.
    • NASA SRTM (30m): Samples elevation and calculates slope steepness.
    • NASA SMAP: Checks topsoil moisture in the first 21 days after sowing to make sure seeds won't dry out.
    • NASA POWER: Analyzes 8 years of historical rainfall, dry spells, and heat waves tied to the crop's actual growth duration.
    • FAO GAEZ v5: Looks up agro-ecological suitability and expected yields.
    • MINAGRI/RAB Soil Data: Evaluates soil pH, texture, and whether lime (ishhwagara) is needed.
  2. Output: The system gives a clear traffic-light result (Feasible, With Concerns, or Infeasible) with straightforward explanations, optimal planting dates, and recommended follow-up crops for rotation.

What benefits does it have?

  • Saves Money & Seeds: Stops farmers from wasting expensive seeds and fertilizer on doomed plantings (e.g., planting rainfed maize during the dry season or on unmanaged steep slopes).
  • Catches False Rainy Season Starts: Uses satellite soil moisture to spot deceptive early rains so seeds don't rot or desiccate in dry soil.
  • No Black Box: Instead of an unexplained score or generative AI guess, every result lists the exact physical reason and numbers behind it.
  • Fast and Lightweight: Uses bundled local rasters and cached data so it runs smoothly even on slower rural internet connections.

What is the intended impact?

Rwanda’s steep hillsides suffer from severe erosion and erratic rainfall. A single failed season can wipe out a smallholder family's income. CropSuite helps farmers protect their harvest, encourages soil-saving practices like bench terracing, and gives agricultural cooperatives and extension agents an evidence-backed tool to guide local communities.

What tools, languages, and software were used?

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn.
  • Geospatial & Data Processing: Rasterio, GDAL, NumPy (for Horn's slope calculation and GeoTIFF sampling).
  • Frontend: Nextjs.
  • Datasets & APIs: NASA SRTM (30m elevation), NASA SMAP (soil moisture), NASA POWER (historical weather), FAO GAEZ v5, MINAGRI soil zones, and Meteomatics (7-day forecast).
  • Testing & Tools: Pytest (41 automated tests covering feasibility rules and APIs), Git, GitLab.

How is the project creative?

Most satellite tools just show complex heatmaps and raw charts that smallholders cannot use. We translated raw satellite data into practical farm rules. For example, instead of just displaying slope degrees, CropSuite checks if the hillside slope exceeds 40%—which violates Rwandan environmental law unless bench terraces (amaterasi y'indinganire) are built. We also anchored historical weather checks to each crop variety's real growing cycle (e.g., 85 days for maize vs. 120 days for beans) rather than a fixed calendar month.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Hilly Topography: Rwanda’s extreme elevation changes (900–2600 m900\text{–}2600\text{ m}900–2600 m) and erosion risks on hillsides.
  • Local Seasons: The three distinct Rwandan agricultural seasons: Season A, Season B, and the dry Season C.
  • Acidic Highland Soils: Widespread high-altitude soil acidity (pH <5.0<5.0<5.0) that stunts crops without agricultural lime.
  • Usability for Farmers: Providing quick district dropdowns for users who don't know their exact GPS coordinates.
  • Core Staple Crops: Focusing on Rwanda's 7 main food security and market staples (maize, beans, sorghum, cassava, Irish potato, sweet potato, and soybean).
